paper_a.title: Dirac's theorem on chordal graphs implies Brooks' theorem

paper_b.title: A short proof of Brooks' theorem

metadata.description: Both papers give short, self-contained proofs of Brooks' theorem but use fundamentally different techniques. Paper A reduces Brooks (in fact a list-coloring strengthening) to a greedy argument on a perfect elimination ordering of chordal graphs (Dirac's theorem), then handles non-chordal graphs by a minimum-counterexample / chordless-cycle reduction with two auxiliary graphs F and H. Paper B argues by induction on |V(G)|: reduce to k-regular, pick non-adjacent neighbors x,y of a vertex v via the absence of K_{k+1}, build a maximal path v_1 v_2 v_3 ... v_r and finish in two cases (r=n and r<n) using a simple PathColor procedure. They also share a generalization angle — paper A proves a list-coloring Brooks (Vizing / Erdos-Rubin-Taylor) while paper B proves a correspondence-coloring Brooks — but the proofs differ at every step.

matches.explanation: Both nodes state Brooks' theorem in the standard form: every connected graph G with maximum degree Delta >= 3 (resp. k>=3), G != K_{Delta+1} (resp. no clique on k+1 vertices), is Delta-colorable (resp. k-colorable). Notation differs (Delta vs k) but the statement is identical, and both are tagged origin: external citing Brooks 1941. This is the shared theorem that makes the pair an alternative-proof pair.

Both papers extend Brooks to a richer coloring framework. Paper A's TP431.3 is the list-coloring Brooks (Vizing; Erdos-Rubin-Taylor): under the same Brooks hypotheses, any list assignment with |L(v)| >= Delta admits an L-coloring. Paper B's TP419.2 is the correspondence-coloring Brooks (Dvorak-Postle setting): the same Brooks hypotheses force, for any constraint graph F on lists of size k, a coloring respecting F. Correspondence coloring strictly generalises list coloring, so the two strengthenings play the same role (a Brooks-type extension proved as the paper's own contribution) but live at different generality levels.

Paper A spells out the basic 'proper k-coloring' definition explicitly. Paper B uses k-coloring throughout but does not lift it to a numbered definition node. This is a granularity difference, not a conceptual gap.

Both papers introduce the standard list-assignment / list-coloring definition (a function L assigning each vertex a list of admissible colors). Paper A has it as a paper-origin definition supporting its list-Brooks strengthening; paper B credits Erdos-Rubin-Taylor 1979 (origin: external). The mathematical object is identical.
Paper A's 'L-colorable' is a separate atomic definition; paper B folds the same notion into its definition of list coloring (DP419.2). Granularity-only mismatch.

Chordal graphs are central to paper A's strategy (Dirac's theorem on chordal graphs supplies the perfect elimination ordering used in Lemma 1). Paper B never invokes chordality — its proof is structured around an induction with maximal paths and a PathColor procedure on arbitrary k-regular graphs. This is a genuine paper-A-specific contribution, signalling the AP route.

The perfect-elimination-ordering definition is essential to paper A's greedy-coloring lemma but has no analogue in paper B, which orders vertices via a maximal path and (in the algorithm) via DFS labels rather than via a clique-elimination structure.

Dirac's chordal-graph theorem (G chordal iff G has a perfect elimination ordering) is the load-bearing external result of paper A — it is even named in paper A's title. Paper B does not cite or use it. This single asymmetry is the strongest evidence of two genuinely different proof techniques.

Paper A's Lemma 1 (list-coloring of chordal graphs by clique number, |L(v)| >= omega suffices) is the engine that turns Dirac into a list-Brooks proof. Paper B has no chordal-graphs lemma; its analogue 'engine' is the PathColor procedure (DP419.1).

Proof of Lemma 1 (greedy coloring along the perfect elimination ordering). Paper B has no greedy-on-PEO step; the analogous 'always pick a free color' move in paper B happens locally inside PathColor. We do not pair these as analogous because the two greedy schemes live in completely different proof skeletons.

These are the two papers' main proofs of (a Brooks-type statement). Paper A: take a minimum counterexample, show by Lemma 1 it is not chordal, find a chordless cycle of length >= 4, build auxiliary graphs F, H, color by minimality, extend along the cycle, contradict. Paper B: induct on |V(G)|, reduce to k-regular, pick non-adjacent neighbors x,y of v (using no K_{k+1}), grow a maximal path v_1 v_2 v_3 ... v_r, split into Case 1 (r=n) and Case 2 (r<n), finish each via PathColor. Same target theorem (Brooks, in its list / plain form), fundamentally different proof strategies — exactly the AP pattern. We also emit the composite step-level entry below to spell out the L2 mismatch.

Composite L2-vs-L2 entry under the parent proof match (PP431.2 ~ PP419.1), as allowed by §Level-2 nodes pattern 1. The two step-DAGs share only the high-level rhythm 'set up an extremal/inductive object, find local structure, finish by a final coloring extension'. Concretely: paper A's minimum-counterexample setup (PSP431.3) plays a similar role to paper B's induction base + reduction to k-regular (PSP419.1); paper A's chordless-cycle extraction (PSP431.4-5) is loosely parallel to paper B's maximal-path extraction (PSP419.2-3); paper A's color-F-by-minimality + extend-around-the-cycle finish (PSP431.7-10) is loosely parallel to paper B's Case-1 and Case-2 PathColor finishes (PSP419.4-6). But the specific moves (auxiliary graphs F, H; residual lists L^*; choosing c_1 to leave >= 2 options at x_2) on the A side have no point-to-point counterpart on the B side, and vice versa (PathColor procedure, decreasing-DFS finish). Hence one composite analogous match rather than per-step matches.

Paper B's PathColor procedure — sequentially greedy-color a path leaving the last vertex uncolored — is the central computational primitive of its proof. Paper A has no such object; its greedy operates along a perfect elimination ordering, not along a path. Paper-B-specific contribution.

Paper B turns its inductive proof into a DFS-based linear-time k-coloring algorithm. Paper A is non-algorithmic. Paper-B-specific contribution. (Algorithm-step children ASP419.1-4 are L2 and intentionally not emitted as 'none'.)

Constraint graph (correspondence coloring) is needed only for paper B's TP419.2 generalization; cited from Dvorak-Postle 2017. Paper A's generalization stays at list-coloring level (no correspondence framework).
'Coloring respecting F' is part of paper B's correspondence-coloring framework only; no analogue in paper A.
Signed-graph proper coloring is invoked only as a special case under paper B's correspondence-coloring Brooks (TP419.2). Paper A has no signed-graph content.
